    "Rich terminal UI does require TTY - line 1597 uses Live() which needs interactive terminal",
    "Analyst 3's quality analysis is well-founded - comprehensive error handling exists throughout (try-catch at 817-823, 926-932, 1114-1116), structured logging to dog.log (198-206), SQLite state persistence for crash recovery (54-121)",

    "Flow control flags (continue_if_failed, skip_if_previous_failed) are real - lines 652-668, 662-668",

  "updated_view": "After reviewing the actual source code, I have a NUANCED view that both validates and contradicts my colleagues' analyses. Dog is architecturally MORE sophisticated than Analyst 2 described but has MORE technical debt than Analyst 3 acknowledged. The critical missed insight is the DUAL-MODE architecture (static flows vs dynamic tasks) that's undergoing active refactoring - this creates complexity and partially explains why some features seem incomplete. The Phase 2.5 evolution (subprocess → Claude API execution) has left DEAD CODE (process monitoring thread lines 834-935 spawns psutil monitoring for subprocesses, but new blocks use Claude API without subprocesses). The CLAUDE.md confirms Phase 3 Go implementation is planned - current Python version should be evaluated as prototype, not production system. Recommendations: (1) Complete task/flow separation refactor, (2) Remove dead subprocess monitoring code, (3) Add comprehensive unit tests before Go migration to preserve business logic, (4) Make validation engine mandatory not optional, (5) Document dual-mode architecture clearly. For Conductor comparison: I cannot access Conductor source code (permission denied), so I can only analyze Dog in depth. If Conductor is shell-based as implied, Dog's Python implementation offers better error handling, state management, and monitoring but at cost of deployment complexity (Python dependencies vs shell portability)."
